title: Yet the consent is supernatural: grace cooperates as a habit with its power
source_text: LXXXV. Nihilominus vult actum liberi arbitrii quo gratiae divinae consentit, non esse mere naturalem, sed supernaturalem; & gratiae Dei tribui debere; Idque non solum quatenus dicitur praeveniens, & hominem allicit & invitat ad bonum, eique quodammodo novas vires sufficit: sed etiam quatenus per eandem gratiam, Deus cum libero hominis arbitrio in actum illius influit, quo respectu dicitur gratia coadjuvans. Nempe, ex ipsius mente, gratia illa Dei qua Deus hominem praevenit, voluntatem in agendo juvat, & cum ea cooperatur, qua ratione habitus potentiae inhaerens, cum illa ad actum ipsius concurrit. Ac proinde illa ipsa gratiae cooperatio a libera voluntate pendet, nec concipi debet ut voluntatem movens & ejus actione prior: quemadmodum influxus habitus in actum aliquem a potentia pendet, nec potentiam ad operandum movet, sed potentia se ad agendum movente simul cum ea in actum potentiae influit.
pass_a_gloss: LXXXV. Nevertheless he wills that the act of free choice by which it consents to divine grace, is not merely natural, but supernatural; and ought to be attributed to the grace of God; And that not only inasmuch as it is called prevenient, and allures and invites man to good, and in some way supplies new strength to him: but also inasmuch as through the same grace, God with the free choice of man flows into its act, in which respect it is called cooperating grace. Namely, from his mind, that grace of God by which God prevents man, helps the will in acting, and cooperates with it, in the way in which a habit inhering in a power, concurs with it to its act. And therefore that very cooperation of grace depends on the free will, nor ought it to be conceived as moving the will and prior to its action: just as the influx of a habit into some act depends on the power, nor does it move the power to working, but the power moving itself to acting it flows together with it into the act of the power.
pass_b_english: Thesis LXXXV. Even so, he holds that the act of free choice by which it consents to divine grace is not merely natural but supernatural, and must be ascribed to God's grace. This is so not only insofar as grace is called prevenient, alluring and inviting a person to the good and in a way supplying him with new strength, but also insofar as through that same grace God, together with man's free choice, flows into its act; in this respect it is called cooperating grace.

On his view, the grace by which God anticipates a person helps the will in acting and cooperates with it in the way a habit inhering in a power concurs with that power toward its act. So this cooperation of grace itself depends on the free will, and must not be thought of as moving the will or as prior to its action. In the same way, a habit's influence on an act depends on the power: the habit does not move the power to act, but, as the power moves itself to act, the habit flows together with it into the power's act.
